title: Indicative vs Subjunctive in Spanish: A Clear Guide

meta_description: Indicative vs subjunctive in Spanish: the indicative states facts, the subjunctive covers wishes, doubts and emotions. Clear triggers, examples and a quiz.
excerpt: Facts on one side, wishes and doubts on the other. A clear way into the Spanish subjunctive.

body_html:
Indicative vs subjunctive is the grammar topic learners fear most, but the idea behind it is simple. The indicative presents something as real: a fact, a certainty, something you are reporting. The subjunctive presents something as not yet real or not asserted: a wish, a request, a doubt, an emotion about something or a possibility. Sé que viene (I know he’s coming) uses the indicative; Espero que venga (I hope he comes) uses the subjunctive, because a hope is not a fact.

Quick answer
  • Indicative = facts and certainty: Creo que tienes razón.
  • Subjunctive = wishes, requests, emotions, doubt and possibility: Quiero que vengas.
  • The subjunctive usually appears after que when the subject changes.
  • Remember WEIRDO: Wishes, Emotions, Impersonal expressions, Recommendations, Doubt, Ojalá.
{{toc}}

Indicative vs subjunctive: the core idea

IndicativeSubjunctive
Sé que está en casa. I know she’s home.Dudo que esté en casa. I doubt she’s home.
Es verdad que llueve. It’s true that it’s raining.Es posible que llueva. It might rain.
Veo que estás cansado. I see you’re tired.Siento que estés cansado. I’m sorry you’re tired.

In each pair, the main clause decides. If it states or reports reality, the second verb is indicative. If it wishes, doubts, reacts emotionally or evaluates, the second verb is subjunctive.

The WEIRDO triggers

  • Wishes: Quiero que me llames. I want you to call me.
  • Emotions: Me alegra que estés aquí. I’m glad you’re here.
  • Impersonal expressions: Es importante que descanses. It’s important that you rest.
  • Recommendations and requests: Te recomiendo que pruebes el mole. I recommend you try the mole.
  • Doubt and denial: No creo que sea verdad. I don’t think it’s true.
  • Ojalá: Ojalá que haga buen tiempo. I hope the weather is nice.

Notice that most of these sentences have two different subjects. When the subject stays the same, Spanish usually uses an infinitive instead: Quiero ir (I want to go), but Quiero que vayas (I want you to go).

{{image:2}}

Creer and pensar: positive vs negative

Creer and pensar are the classic trap. In positive sentences they express belief, which Spanish treats as close to fact, so they take the indicative: Creo que es buena idea. In negative sentences they express doubt, so they take the subjunctive: No creo que sea buena idea.

The same happens with es verdad que, es cierto que and es obvio que: indicative when positive, subjunctive when negative.

Cuando and other time words

After cuando, en cuanto, hasta que and después de que, the tense depends on time. For habits or the past, use the indicative: Cuando llego a casa, ceno. When I get home, I have dinner. For the future, use the subjunctive, because it hasn’t happened yet: Cuando llegues a casa, llámame. When you get home, call me.

This is one of the most common mistakes I see, because English uses the present in both cases.

Words that always take the subjunctive

A few connectors trigger the subjunctive every time, because they introduce something that hasn’t happened or isn’t real: para que (so that), antes de que (before), sin que (without), a menos que (unless) and con tal de que (as long as).

  • Te lo explico para que lo entiendas. I’ll explain it so that you understand.
  • Sal antes de que empiece a llover. Leave before it starts raining.
  • No voy a menos que vengas tú. I’m not going unless you come.
{{book:the-mind-lies}}

How to start learning the subjunctive

Many learners try to memorize every rule at once and give up. A gentler path works better:

  1. Learn the forms of the present subjunctive with a handful of common verbs: sea, esté, tenga, vaya, haga, pueda.
  2. Collect fixed phrases like que te vaya bien and ojalá que sí, and use them in real messages.
  3. Add one trigger a week: first quiero que, then espero que, then cuando with the future.
  4. Notice it while reading. Every time you see a subjunctive form, ask why the writer chose it.

Within a few months, the subjunctive stops being a chapter in a grammar book and becomes part of how you speak.

The subjunctive in everyday phrases

You probably already use the subjunctive in fixed phrases without noticing:

  • ¡Que te vaya bien! Hope it goes well!
  • ¡Que te mejores! Get well soon!
  • ¡Que tengas un buen día! Have a good day!
  • ¡Que descanses! Rest well!
  • Como quieras. As you wish.

Each is a wish, with the main verb (“I hope”) left unsaid. These are a gentle way to start, and you will find many of them in {{link:get-well-soon-in-spanish|get well soon in Spanish}} and {{link:birthday-wishes-in-spanish|birthday wishes in Spanish}}.

{{image:3}}

Common mistakes

  • Quiero que tú vienes. A wish about someone else: Quiero que vengas.
  • No creo que es verdad. Negative belief: No creo que sea verdad.
  • Cuando llegas mañana, llámame. Future after cuando: Cuando llegues mañana, llámame.
  • Espero que vienes. Hope is a wish: Espero que vengas.

The Real Academia Española explains every use of the subjunctive in the Diccionario panhispánico de dudas, which is worth bookmarking for doubtful cases.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Indicative vs subjunctive becomes much less scary once you see it as one question: am I stating something as real, or not? Start with the fixed phrases, then the WEIRDO triggers, then cuando with the future. You don’t need to master it all at once. For the other pairs that cause the same kind of doubt, see {{link:spanish-confusing-words|Spanish confusing words}}.

faq.q: What is the difference between the indicative and the subjunctive?
faq.a: The indicative presents facts and certainty. The subjunctive presents wishes, requests, emotions, doubts and possibilities that are not asserted as fact.
Wishes, Emotions, Impersonal expressions, Recommendations, Doubt and Ojalá: the main triggers of the subjunctive.
No. Creo que takes the indicative. No creo que takes the subjunctive.

faq.q: Do Spanish speakers use the subjunctive every day?
faq.a: Constantly. Phrases like que te vaya bien, cuando llegues and espero que estés bien are part of everyday conversation.

questions.explain: A wish about someone else: subjunctive.
A negative belief expresses doubt: subjunctive.
